implementation_notes: Sequel ships the pattern as a plugin: plugin :class_table_inheritance, key: :kind makes the root model's table the base and gives every subclass model its own table whose id is a foreign key to the root's id (the docs' example: employees(id, name, kind), staff and managers each with id referencing employees.id). What replaces the classic mapper is the plugin plus the lazy_attributes plugin it installs: subclass datasets are built as a subquery joining the path (CEO.all reads employees JOIN managers JOIN executives) and subclass columns missing from a superclass load are fetched lazily. Composing the tables by hand is only worth it on ActiveRecord.
pitfalls: No subclass table may repeat a column name from a superclass table - the plugin does not support overlapping names, so a column has to move to the table of the class that actually owns it.

Subclass datasets read from a subquery, so inserts/updates/deletes must be driven through the tables (cti_tables), and qualified identifiers must address the subquery alias rather than the base table name.

variants.name: ActiveRecord composition with has_one/belongs_to
variants.idiom_name: belongs_to/has_one on the shared key plus delegation
variants.implementation_notes: ActiveRecord has no joined-inheritance mapper: the Rails associations guide documents single table inheritance and delegated types, not this strategy, so on Rails the pattern is composed by hand - the base model is a table, each subtype is its own model whose primary key is the base key (self.primary_key), and the public API delegates to the subtype record or uses delegated_type. What replaces the classic mapper is association code plus delegation, and polymorphic reads become one query per kind. Choose it when the application is already Rails-shaped and the hierarchy is small.
variants.code_sketch:
class Party < ApplicationRecord; end

class Person < ApplicationRecord
  self.primary_key = :id       # people.id is also the FK to parties.id
  belongs_to :party
  delegate :name, to: :party
end
# read one type: Person.joins(:party).find(id)
pitfalls: belongs_to on a column that is also the primary key needs self.primary_key explicitly, otherwise Rails treats the record as a child with a generated key and the join breaks.

Mixing this composition with a type column on the base table makes ActiveRecord apply single table inheritance and raise for subclasses that have no table of their own; keep the composed form free of that column.
